text: February 1995. In Singapore, a 27-year-old trader leaves a note behind. Two words. I'm sorry. Then he disappears. Three days later, one of the oldest banks in Britain collapses. Bearings. 233 years old. A bank that helped the United States by Louisiana. A bank that reportedly counted the Queen among its clients. And a few days after that, it sold for 1 pound, 1, British, pound, the price of a cup of coffee. So how does one guy in his 20s sink a bank that's older than the United States? The answer involves a lucky number, an earthquake, and a secret account that nobody bothered to open. London, 1762. France is bearing opens a small merchant bank. Over the next decades, it becomes one of the most powerful banks on the planet. In 1803, Bearing's helps finance the Louisiana purchase. America doubles in size and a London bank helps pay the bill. In 1818, a French statesman, the Duke de Richelieu, said there were six great powers in Europe. England, France, Prussia, Austria, Russia, and the Bearing Brothers. Translation, a bank ranked right next to empires. But Bearing's had already almost died once. In 1890, bad bets in Argentina nearly sank it and the Bank of England organized a rescue. Remember that. It matters later. By the 1990s, bearings is an elegant, very British bank, old portraits, old money, old habits, and it wants some new money. So it moves into a faster, riskier business, derivatives trading in Asia. Translation, betting on where markets will go, using contracts that can multiply your gains or your losses. Enter Nick Leason, born in 1967 near London, the son of a plasterer, no university degree. He joins bearings in 1989 in the back office. Translation, the people who check the trades and do the paperwork. Not glamorous, but he's good at it. In 1992, bearings sent him to Singapore to run its futures business on the Singapore Exchange, CMEX. Futures, translation, contracts to buy or sell something later at a price fixed today. And here's the problem. Leason runs the trading. And he also runs the back office. The people who are supposed to check the trading. Translation, the student is grading his own exam. Who checks Nick's trades? The back office. And who runs the back office? Nick. Perfect. Next item. In July 1992, an error account is opened in Singapore. Number 888888. Translation. An error account is a little drawer where a bank park smokes the stakes until they're fixed. And 8 is a lucky number in Chinese culture. Five eights? That's very lucky. Spoiler? Not that lucky. According to Leeson, it starts with a colleague's mistake, about 20,000 pounds. He hides it in the drawer. Then he starts hiding his own losing trades there too. By the end of 1992, the drawer holds about 2 million pounds of losses. Meanwhile, on paper, he's a superstar. In 1993, he reportedly makes more than 10 million pounds for bearings, about 10% of the whole bank's profit. His bonus, around 130,000 pounds on top of a 50,000 pound salary. In London, he's the golden boy. And nobody asks how he does it, because when someone makes you that much money, asking questions feels rude. In 1994, an internal audit even warned that Leicyn controlled both the trading and the back office. Its advice split the two jobs. It never really happened. The report went into a drawer. Not the lucky one, but still a drawer. But every time he loses, he bets bigger to win it back. Translation. The strategy of everyone who ever said just one more hand at a casino. By the end of 1994, the lucky drawer is hiding 208 million pounds. Then came the earthquake. In January 1995, Leeson has a huge bet on Japan's stock market, the Nike, a short straddle. Translation, he's betting the market stays calm. If it barely moves, he wins a little. If it moves a lot, in any direction, he can lose a lot. On January 17th, at 5.46 in the morning, a massive earthquake hits Kobe, Japan. More than 6,000 people die. And Japan's stock market drops. A normal trader cuts his losses. Leicyn does the opposite. He buys more and more Nike futures, betting the market will bounce back. One man in Singapore trying to hold up the Japanese stock market by himself. To keep his positions open, he needs cash. So London keeps sending money to Singapore, hundreds of millions of pounds. Singapore needs more money. How much? A lot. For what? Client, apparently. Well, Nick knows what he's doing. The market doesn't bounce back. February 23rd, 1995. Leeson leaves the office, leaves his note, and flees with his wife, Lisa, across the border into Malaysia, then a luxury resort in Borneo. On February 25th, he turns 28. Happy birthday! The next day, February 26th, bearings collapses. The total loss? About 827 million pounds, roughly $1.3 billion, more than the bank's entire capital. Translation? Everything the bank had was not enough to cover what one man lost. And remember 1890? This time the bank of England looks for a rescue and can't find one. On March 2nd, Leeson lands in Frankfurt. The German police are waiting for him. Days later the Dutch group ING buys bearings for 1 pound. Then, it pumps in about 660 million pounds to keep it alive. The sixth great power of Europe for the price of a candy bar. So, what happened to Nick? He's sent back to Singapore. In December 1995, he sentenced to 6 and a half years in Changi Prison. In prison, he's diagnosed with colon cancer. He survives it, and he's released in July 1999. His wife divorces him. He writes a book called Rogue Trader. It becomes a movie starring Ivan McGregor. And today, he gives talks to companies about risk. The man who broke the bank now explains how not to break the bank. And in 2018, he even joined celebrity big brother. And the bearings name? It survived. Today, bearings is an investment firm based in Charlotte, North Carolina, owned by an American insurance company. The bank that helped America buy Louisiana is now, well, American. So what's the lesson? It wasn't just one rogue trader. It was a bank that let one man make trades and check his own trades. A bank that never asked how a 20-something made 10% of its profits. And a bank that kept sending him millions without asking why. When something makes you too much money to question, that's exactly when you should question it. 8888. The luckiest number in the world. Until someone opens the drawer. If you enjoyed this, subscribe. Next time, the hedge fund run by Nobel Prize winners that lost $4.6 billion in a few months and needed Wall Street to save it.
